Issued at 1256 AM CDT Thu Sep 17 2026

The latest RAP analysis and satellite/radar imagery show light 
rain spreading east across northern Wisconsin within the right 
entrance region of a 150 kt jet streak and ahead of a positively 
tilted shortwave. A cluster of thunderstorms is pushing east 
across west-central Wisconsin on the nose of an elevated moisture 
transport axis and moisture convergence. Instability is nearly nil
across northeast Wisconsin, so expectations are for this cluster 
of storms to diminish prior to reaching central Wisconsin. At the 
surface, high pressure is centered over the northern Plains, while
the next weather system for Friday is currently impacting the 
central Rockies. 

Early Morning Showers and Quiet Weather Tonight: The ongoing 
showers will continue to track east across northern Wisconsin 
early this morning and provide up to a quarter inch of 
precipitation. Clouds with spotty showers will likely stick around
for much of the morning, particularly across east-central 
Wisconsin where low-level moisture is most plentiful, before 
partial clearing occurs in the afternoon. High temperatures will 
be seasonable today, ranging from the upper 60s to middle 70s. 
Relatively quiet weather is expected tonight as the surface high 
pressure builds into the region. Patchy fog may develop over far 
northeast Wisconsin late tonight, before mid and high clouds above
15 kft begin to increase from west to east overnight ahead of our
next system.

Heavy Rainfall Potential Friday into Saturday: High pressure 
departs the region on Friday morning as shortwave energy and 
associated low pressure move across the central Plains. Rain 
within a strong frontogenesis region on the nose of a 30 to 40 kt 
low-level jet looks to spread into north-central Wisconsin as 
early as late Friday morning, which is slightly earlier than 
forecast yesterday, before spreading across the rest of the area 
in the afternoon. The heaviest rain will likely fall on Friday 
night as impressive dynamics in the right rear quadrant of a jet 
streak, mid-level frontogenesis, and moisture convergence align 
above the returning warm front. Precipitable water values are 
forecast to climb to 1.80 inches, pushing into the 98th percentile
for mid-September. Deep warm cloud depths over 12 kft will lead 
to efficient rainfall production. The risk for severe 
thunderstorms is low, with most unstable CAPE values only up to 
500 j/kg. 

Confidence in heavy rainfall has held steady over the 
past 24 hours. Probabilities of rainfall in excess of 2 inches 
generally range from 40 to 60 percent south of Wausau and Green 
Bay, roughly south of Highway 29. However, there has been a slight
southward shift in the axis of heaviest rainfall in the latest 
model runs. It is common for the heaviest rainfall to be displaced
southward from consensus model guidance, making the exact 
location of the heaviest rainfall one of the greatest 
uncertainties with this forecast. There will also likely be a 
rather sharp cutoff to the northern edge of the precipitation 
shield, so far northern Wisconsin may see considerably less rain 
than current forecasts indicate. 

In terms of flooding impacts, the EFI has held steady across 
central and east-central Wisconsin. Probabilities of reaching 
flash flood guidance are generally under 10 percent in a 6-hour 
period, so the potential for flash flooding looks isolated at 
best. This will behave more as a long- duration rainfall event 
that will lead to stream and river rises, accumulating water in 
low-lying areas such as ditches and culverts, and ponding of water
on roads. The heaviest rainfall is projected to impact some of 
the same areas that received 1 to 3 inches of rain earlier in the 
week and are the areas that will be most susceptible localized
flooding. The rain will likely end for most locations by Saturday
evening.

Marine and Beach Hazards Friday Night through Sunday: Gusty 
easterly winds ahead of and during the passage of the 
aforementioned low pressure system will build wave heights 
significantly on Lake Michigan from Friday night through the 
weekend. This will create hazardous conditions for small craft and
increase the risk for dangerous rip currents along area beaches 
through at least Sunday and possibly into Monday.

Quiet Weather Pattern Next Week: Shortwave energy from the 
western North American trough will slowly migrate east over the 
center of the country through the middle of next week. The 
associated low pressure system and rainfall footprint have trended
further south over the past 24 hours. Therefore, it appears that 
the bulk of the precipitation will remain south of the region. 
Only small chances of rain, up to 30 percent, are forecast for 
Monday. For the remainder of the week, strong high pressure
